Patients with GT have spontaneous, lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding as epistaxis, menorrhagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, and gingival bleeding (Figure 1) [6]. The patients usually have chronic gingivitis and periodontal disease associated with chronic blood loss. Patients with GT are usually are hesitant to brush their teeth and are generally poorly compliant in dental maintenance, despite therapeutic education focused on dental hygiene [7,8]. findings.label: Ecchymoses
findings.evidence: Ecchymoses (arrows) of the lower limbs in our case of Glanzmann thrombasthenia

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the lower limbs showing multiple ecchymoses (arrows), captioned explicitly as being from the authors' case of Glanzmann thrombasthenia; in-text mentions multiple ecchymoses predominantly on the lower limbs in this patient. Real patient photograph showing a specific mucocutaneous bleeding manifestation of the target disease, so it is included. Age group taken from the article title/in-text (14-month-old infant).
panels.attribution_text: Chemlal et al. Glanzmann Thrombasthenia in a 14-Month-Old Infant: A Rare Platelet Function Disorder Presenting With Persistent Mucocutaneous Bleeding.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.108835. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Ecchymoses (arrows) of the lower limbs in our case of Glanzmann thrombasthenia
in_text_mentions: On admission, the patient was alert and stable, with slightly pale conjunctivae. Physical examination revealed active gingival bleeding at the upper central incisor, a bruise on the lower lip, and multiple ecchymoses predominantly on the lower limbs (Figure 1), along with older lesions on the trunk. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy was detected, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.
